title: seekdb in one paragraph
text: seekdb is an AI-native search database that answers questions you would normally ask a search engine. It keeps dense vectors, sparse vectors and relational columns in one engine, so a single SQL-compatible service can do semantic similarity, keyword matching and ranked fusion. Because it speaks the MySQL wire protocol, ordinary clients and ORMs connect without a special SDK, while native vector columns are still available for approximate nearest neighbour search.

title: Embedded mode versus server mode
text: seekdb ships in two deployment shapes. Embedded mode runs the engine inside your own process: you point the client at a local directory and no network service is started, which is convenient on a laptop or in a CI job. Server mode connects over the MySQL protocol to a listening host and port, typically 127.0.0.1:2881 during local development. Embedded mode needs a native binary for the current platform, so Windows users normally run server mode instead.

title: Collections and vector indexes
text: A collection is the unit of storage for a knowledge base. When you create one you declare the embedding dimension and the distance metric, for example dimension 384 with cosine distance. The engine builds a dense vector index over the declared column, a full-text index over the document text, and optionally a sparse index for BM25 style scoring. Querying the collection returns ids, documents, metadata and distance values.

title: Cosine distance and inner product
text: Cosine distance measures the angle between two vectors and ignores their magnitudes, so it is the usual choice for sentence embeddings that have already been length normalised. Inner product is cheaper to compute and equals cosine similarity when both vectors are unit length. Euclidean distance grows with magnitude differences and is rarely the best choice for normalised text embeddings. Pick one metric at collection creation time and keep queries consistent with it.

title: Full-text indexes and tokenizers
text: The full-text side of the engine tokenises documents and query strings into terms, then matches them with an inverted index. Chinese text needs a word segmenter such as IK with a smart or maximum-word mode, while English relies on whitespace and punctuation splitting with case folding. A full-text index answers exact term lookups that embeddings often blur, including rare identifiers, error codes and product names.

title: Reciprocal rank fusion explained
text: Reciprocal rank fusion combines several ranked lists without needing calibrated scores. Each document receives the sum over lists of one divided by a constant plus its rank in that list, so a document that is ranked highly by both the keyword branch and the vector branch rises to the top. RRF never compares raw similarity numbers, which makes it robust when the two branches produce incomparable score distributions.

title: BM25 sparse scoring
text: BM25 scores a document for a query by summing term frequency saturation and inverse document frequency, then normalising by document length. Two tuning knobs, usually written k1 and b, control how quickly repeated terms stop helping and how strongly long documents are penalised. A sparse BM25 index complements dense embeddings because it rewards exact rare terms while embeddings capture paraphrase.

title: Transformers.js overview
text: Transformers.js runs Hugging Face models directly in JavaScript. It converts model weights to ONNX and executes them with ONNX Runtime, either in the browser or in Node. The library exposes a pipeline helper so that feature extraction, text generation and other tasks need only a few lines of code. No server, GPU cluster or Python runtime is required, and the same API works on WebGPU, WASM and native CPU execution providers.

title: ONNX Runtime Web and the WASM backend
text: The WASM backend compiles ONNX graphs to WebAssembly and runs them on the CPU. It works in every modern browser, needs no special flags, and can use multiple threads when cross-origin isolation is configured. Its weakness is raw throughput: matrix multiplications for a transformer encoder are several times slower than on a discrete GPU. It is the dependable fallback whenever hardware acceleration is missing.

title: WebGPU acceleration in the browser
text: WebGPU exposes a modern graphics and compute API to web pages, and ONNX Runtime can map transformer operators onto it for large speedups over CPU execution. A page can only obtain an adapter in a secure context, so https or localhost is required, and some browsers or virtual machines return a null adapter even when the API exists. Production code must therefore probe for a working adapter and fall back gracefully.

title: INT8 quantization
text: Eight-bit quantization stores weights as integers with a per-channel scale and zero point, cutting the memory footprint to roughly a quarter of a float32 model. For a small sentence encoder this turns a ninety megabyte checkpoint into something closer to twenty five megabytes, which matters on mobile networks. Retrieval quality usually drops by only a point or two of recall because sentence embeddings are robust to small weight perturbations.

title: FP16 half precision
text: Half precision keeps the floating point format but halves the number of bits per weight, giving a two to one compression relative to float32. It is the natural choice on GPUs that have fast native fp16 arithmetic, and it degrades quality far less than eight bit integer quantization. On CPUs, however, fp16 may be emulated and therefore slower than int8 kernels that use vectorised integer instructions.

title: MiniLM sentence encoder
text: MiniLM-L6-v2 is a six layer distilled transformer that maps a sentence to a 384 dimensional vector. It is small enough to download and run in a browser tab, and it remains a strong baseline for semantic search on English text. The model was distilled from a larger teacher on paraphrase and natural language inference objectives, which is why it captures sentence level meaning rather than exact wording.

title: Mean pooling and normalisation
text: A sentence embedding pipeline first tokenises the input, runs the encoder, then reduces the token vectors to one vector per sentence. Mean pooling averages the token states while respecting the attention mask so padding tokens are ignored. Length normalisation afterwards projects the vector onto the unit sphere, which makes cosine distance and inner product agree and keeps scores comparable across inputs of different length.

title: Latency and memory on edge devices
text: On a mid-range laptop the native CPU backend encodes a short sentence in roughly ten to twenty milliseconds, while WebGPU can bring that down to a few milliseconds once the pipeline is warmed up. The dominant cost for a first run is the model download, not inference. Memory matters too: a quantized encoder plus the attention workspace typically stays well under two hundred megabytes of resident memory.

title: Caching models in the browser
text: Transformers.js stores downloaded weights in the browser cache and reuses them across page loads, so the second visit does not re-download anything. Programmatic control is available through the environment object, which can disable local model lookups, choose a remote host, or turn caching off entirely for debugging. Warm caches make cold start essentially a deserialisation cost of a few hundred milliseconds.

title: Evaluating retrieval with Recall at K
text: Recall at K asks what fraction of the truly relevant documents appear in the first K results, averaged over a set of queries that carry hand labelled relevance judgments. It is the standard sanity check for a retrieval pipeline because it ignores the ordering inside the cut-off. Mean reciprocal rank and normalised discounted cumulative gain add ranking sensitivity, but recall at five and at ten are the numbers most teams report first.

title: Chunking long documents
text: Long documents must be split before embedding, because a sentence encoder truncates at a few hundred tokens and a single vector cannot represent an entire chapter. Splitting on blank lines or headings preserves natural boundaries, and a hard character cap prevents any single chunk from exceeding the model limit. Overlapping windows help when a fact straddles a boundary but multiply storage cost.

title: Hybrid search versus pure vector search
text: Pure vector search is forgiving about wording but weak on exact strings such as error codes, version numbers or surnames. A hybrid query runs the keyword branch and the vector branch, then merges the two ranked lists, which recovers exact matches while keeping semantic recall. In practice hybrid retrieval beats either branch alone on mixed workloads, at the price of one extra index to maintain.

title: Incremental import and document identity
text: Knowledge bases grow over time, so the import path must append rather than rebuild. A stable document identifier is what makes repeated imports safe: re-running an import with the same ids either updates in place or can be skipped, and a fresh session can still find everything that was written earlier. Generating a new identifier per run gives append-only behaviour that never destroys existing rows.

title: HNSW graph parameters
text: Hierarchical navigable small world graphs index vectors as a layered proximity graph. The parameter M fixes how many neighbours each node keeps, which directly trades recall for memory, while efConstruction controls how hard the builder searches and therefore index quality. A larger efSearch at query time raises recall at the cost of latency, so these three knobs form the main recall and speed dial.

title: Secure contexts and feature detection
text: Several browser capabilities are restricted to secure contexts, meaning https or a localhost origin. WebGPU is one of them: on a plain http page served from a LAN address the navigator.gpu property can be missing entirely. Robust applications therefore feature detect rather than sniff user agents, and report the chosen execution backend in the interface so that users understand why performance differs.

title: Retrieval augmented generation in brief
text: Retrieval augmented generation pairs a search step with a language model. The retriever fetches passages relevant to the question, the passages are inserted into the prompt, and the model answers grounded in that context. Almost all of the answer quality comes from the retriever, so it is worth measuring recall before tuning the generator. In an offline knowledge base the retriever is the only component that must run locally.

title: SQL compatibility and relational joins
text: Because the engine is MySQL compatible, you can keep ordinary relational tables next to vector collections and join across them. A typical pattern runs a vector or hybrid query to obtain a ranked list of ids, then selects the matching rows from a relational table with an IN clause, merging the two results in application code. This keeps rich business data out of the vector store while still supporting semantic retrieval.
